title: Lecture 5. Trends in the development of the prevention system in the modern world
summary:
📋 Main Lecture Topics
  1. Demographic Changes
  2. Cultural Changes
  3. Labor Market Changes
  4. Changes in the Education System
  5. Societal Changes
  6. Changes in Physical and Mental Health Patterns
  7. Changes in Child Rearing Strategies
  8. Policy on Deviant Behavior
  9. Three Prevention Strategies
  10. Prevention of Delinquency (Criminal Behavior) in Adolescents
  11. Principles of (Social) Marketing
  12. Models of Behavior Change

1. Demographic Changes Throughout human history, relatively few people lived on Earth compared to today. Only in the last 200-300 years has there been an explosive growth in population. When the adult readers of these lines were born, the number of people on Earth was probably between 4 and 5 billion. When modern teenagers were born, approximately 6.5 billion people lived on Earth. And now there are already 8 billion of us. Such a rapid change in the demographic situation could not but affect all aspects of people's lives, including the understanding of such key concepts as happiness, health, psychological well-being, life success, the meaning of life…

Demographic transition — stabilization of population size due to a decrease in birth and death rates.

  • Modernization, growth of GDP per capita.
  • Urbanization: a large number of children (labor, reproduction), which was beneficial in an agrarian society, loses its meaning in the city (low infant mortality, high population density, high costs for raising and educating children, pension reform)
  • Increased life expectancy, increased average age.

2. Cultural Changes We live in an amazing time when many things in human history are happening for the first time. Once upon a time, a grandfather holding his grandson knew his fate. It was obvious that the grandson would exactly repeat the fate of his father and grandfather. Today, our lives are very different from the lives of our parents. And the lives of our children will be largely unlike ours. Therefore, today the experience of previous generations no longer plays the decisive role it once did. New generations can no longer simply copy the lives of their parents and rely on their experience, as was the case before. The traditional culture of an agrarian society is built on the preceding generation passing its experience to the next. For the first time in human history, the next generation knows more than the previous one. Previously, experience was more important than creativity; creativity is becoming more important than experience. Adults don't quite understand what needs to be taught, and learning proceeds in reverse.

3. Labor Market Changes The labor market is changing; new professions are appearing and disappearing before our eyes, so people today have to learn throughout their lives, rather than acquiring one profession once and for all. Intangible products – information – are gaining increasing importance. Informatization, artificial intelligence, recognition systems, and big data analysis open up new opportunities for job automation. Professions where humans are indispensable will remain in demand. Therefore, for a successful life, not only professional skills but also personal qualities and socio-psychological competencies such as self-confidence, conflict resolution skills, teamwork ability, initiative, creativity, leadership qualities, and many others are becoming important.

Means of production are changing. If previously a career was only possible within organizations, and more often large organizations, today anyone can earn money from home, being a freelancer or self-employed.

4. Changes in the Education System Previously, a person received an education and then used the acquired knowledge throughout their life. Today, knowledge becomes outdated faster than it appears in curricula. Therefore, people learn throughout their lives, and begin learning immediately in a work situation

Therefore, the education system in all countries is currently undergoing a rapid period of reform. The main trend of these reforms is that the student becomes an active participant in the learning process, rather than just a recipient of information. To master modern educational programs, it is no longer enough to simply transmit knowledge from teacher to student. Modern education is a product of cooperation between teacher and student, based not on coercion and fear of bad grades, but on the student's own motivation to acquire new knowledge.

The implementation of modern education's pedagogical tasks simultaneously involves creating psychological and pedagogical conditions for preserving and strengthening health, and forming a dignified life perspective for each student. This is impossible without the child possessing psychological knowledge about themselves, their personal and age-related characteristics, rules for competent interaction with others, skills for acting in difficult life situations, positive thinking, and principles of a healthy lifestyle, corresponding to their individual capabilities and needs.

Health protection has long ceased to be solely the responsibility of the healthcare system. Currently, a comprehensive approach to understanding health prevails in social sciences, which includes mental, spiritual, emotional, social, and physical health, all interacting with each other and determining well-being at the level of the individual, social groups, and society as a whole.

5. Societal Changes Property. GDP growth leads to it becoming cheaper and more convenient not to own property, but to rent it. If previously social status was ensured by wealth and accumulation, today wealthy people lead a distinctly modest lifestyle and make do with the necessary minimum.

Personalization of responsibility. Institutions of social control, characteristic of traditional societies, are giving way to personal responsibility for life, upbringing, and recovery. There is a shift from a collective to an individualistically oriented value system and a corresponding change in behavioral norms.

Meaning of life. Previously, people tried to avoid physical labor and stay at home, because labor and wandering were a curse and the lot of the lower classes. Today we travel, climb mountains, exhaust ourselves with training, and strive to travel more. Because adventure becomes the main drive. Profitable and reliable investment items are no longer things and property, but new experiences and good relationships with family and friends.

Participation in public life. In the transition from traditional to (post)industrial society, a new type of social connection between people is formed, based on individual choice. If previously social activity was a hobby for a small part of the population, now it is an indicator of social maturity, which is increasingly valued.

6. Changes in Physical and Mental Health Patterns Shift from infectious diseases to chronic ones due to:

urbanization (improved quality of life), healthcare systems (industrialization), transition from traditional to industrial society, discovery of antibiotics (1928 A. Fleming, penicillin), increase in average life expectancy (from 35 to 70 years).

Changing health standards. Before: rich – fat, poor – thin. Now it's the opposite. A healthy lifestyle, weight control – this is not only a matter of health but also a reflection of the spirit of the times. If 50 years ago smoking was fashionable, now it's a healthy lifestyle.

Increase in anxiety and depression levels in the population. The personalization of responsibility and the uncertainty of the future lead to high levels of chronic stress. This occurs against the backdrop of the loss of the therapeutic role of traditional societies.

Increased demand for psychology. Rising stress levels, on the one hand, and a high standard of living, on the other, compel people to pay more attention to their emotions and psychological well-being. Thus, with changes in the understanding of causality in medical science, there is a shift from bio-reductionism to a holistic approach.

7. Changes in Child Rearing Strategies Today, raising a healthy personality requires greater effort from parents than in previous times. This is due to the rapid complication of social relations, to which we are all forced to adapt, and to the increasing role of personal qualities necessary for this adaptation.

Once, the upbringing process implied only a one-sided transfer of experience from adults to children, where children were only required to conform to certain behavioral norms and master a narrow range of academic and professional skills. Raising a healthy, adaptive personality in today's world implies that the child is also an active participant in the upbringing process. Today's upbringing strategy focuses on stimulating the child's own activity and awareness: self-understanding, the ability to express their thoughts and desires, curiosity for independent exploration of the surrounding world, forming experience in making independent decisions, making mistakes, and finding ways to overcome their consequences.

Separation, as a result of healthy maturation, is the main educational goal. This applies not only to parents but also to all specialists working with minors. Below is a model of child upbringing that includes three directions ensuring healthy separation, which parents should understand and specialists working with children should keep in mind in their daily activities:

Care for the child's emotional sphere; Opportunities and limitations of the surrounding world; Formation of independent behavior.

8. Policy on Deviant Behavior In your practice of counseling adolescents, you have surely encountered situations where you had to carefully weigh information so that it would not harm them, but at the same time influence their behavior in the desired direction. For example, if you tell an adolescent about drugs within the ideology of "zero tolerance" – that all drugs are equally dangerous, that they all kill immediately, that only very bad people use them – you risk completely losing their trust, because they have their own experience interacting with peers who use drugs. And the adolescent knows that all these categorical statements cannot be true, that reality is more complex, and they want to understand precisely that complexity. They see you as a specialist and trust you until the moment you speak falsehoods or unsubstantiated information. This example demonstrates the counter-current faced by authors of prevention programs on topics such as substance abuse prevention, sex education for the prevention of early pregnancy and venereal diseases, and similar issues. As a result, two conflicting approaches have emerged, adhered to by two "camps" of specialists. The first advocates for restricting adolescents from information. Their main argument is that the effects of complex social interventions, such as prevention programs, are indeed difficult to calculate and guarantee a reduction in risks rather than an increase. And indeed, an analysis of the results of numerous programs for the prevention of drug use, teenage pregnancies, and venereal diseases showed that, alongside positive effects, such programs also carry risks, namely provoking adolescents' interest in the behaviors to which the programs are dedicated. However, a preventive approach based on restricting information for adolescents essentially boils down to transmitting generally accepted norms of morality and law. And all would be well, but adolescents are thereby deprived of the opportunity for conscious choice and are left alone with the true causes of their risky behavior: with their emotions, cognitive distortions, and the lifestyle they have already become involved in. And this fact itself can lead to even more unpredictable consequences than violating moral norms, for example, depression and suicides. Therefore, the second "camp" of specialists, on the contrary, advocates for providing adolescents with full information about the problem within the framework of legalization policy.

Three strategies for preventing deviant behavior can be identified: Prohibition (ban) Legalization (regulation) Abolitionism (absence of prohibition or regulation) Trends in social control policy over deviant behavior: recognition of the failure of repression ("crisis of punishment"); changing social control strategy from "struggle" and "war" to "peaceful coexistence"; searching for social control measures alternative to repressive ones; priority of prevention.

9. Three Prevention Strategies Using drug policy as an example, three focuses, and accordingly, three prevention strategies can be identified: Demand reduction: all prevention, and primarily its primary level, is aimed at preventing people from turning to drugs. Supply reduction: the less available a substance is (represented on the market), the fewer its consumers will be. Supply reduction is ensured by legislative restrictions on the sale of tobacco, alcohol, and the circulation of narcotic substances, as well as by the activities of the law enforcement system. Harm reduction proceeds from the recognition of the inevitability of consumption by some part of society, for example, tobacco, alcohol, or drugs, and is therefore aimed at reducing the negative consequences of their use. Measures of such prevention include: providing sterile injection equipment, seat belts (reducing the negative consequences of car use), condoms (reducing the negative consequences of sexual contacts), creams with UV protection (reducing the negative consequences of sun exposure), etc.

10. Prevention of Delinquency (Criminal Behavior) in Adolescents Over the last century, the system for preventing juvenile delinquency worldwide has undergone rapid theoretical and practical development, resulting in a shift of focus from punishment to support and social rehabilitation for juvenile offenders. At the same time, public and professional discussions have sought to find an optimal solution to the contradiction between the demands of public safety, the main of which is to reduce criminal risks, on the one hand, and fair justice for youth, on the other. Fair justice is understood as its attention to circumstances that naturally distinguish adolescents from adults, such as: insufficient understanding of social norms, undeveloped legal and civic consciousness, insufficient development of brain regions that inhibit emotional impulses, and the natural tendency of adolescents to experiment with new forms of behavior.

The central idea of preventing criminal behavior in adolescents has been the attempt to develop in them the social knowledge and skills necessary for performing adult social roles in society, including full legal responsibility for their actions. Research results show that efforts to develop skills in young people for establishing close relationships, cooperating in groups, planning their lives, resolving conflicts, self-reliance, making informed decisions, and taking responsibility for their actions have a greater impact on reducing recidivism – the main indicator of the success of the offense prevention system – than stricter punishment.

11. Principles of (Social) Marketing As mentioned above, the main goal of preventing chronic diseases and all types of behavioral disorders is to reduce the level of stress experienced by individuals and social groups. This circumstance emphasizes that a person cannot be forced to be healthy, but their own natural desire for it can be developed and supported. Therefore, modern healthcare applies the principles of a marketing approach, the same as in commercial projects. In both cases, they are focused on changing behavior – in one case, consumer behavior, in the other, health-related behavior.

Principles of the social marketing concept: Consumer orientation. As in commercial marketing, collecting information about the consumer, their preferences, attitudes, lifestyle, and social context is key to promoting a particular product (in our case – ideas, attitudes, lifestyles, behavioral patterns). Existing behavioral patterns and goals for changing behavioral patterns. The key here will be identifying factors that contribute to behavior change or the formation of desired behavior. Diverse interventions. To form sustainable changes in behavioral patterns, a combination of different approaches is necessary. Interventions based on only one intervention are rarely successful. Audience segmentation. Social groups whose health-related behavior we would like to influence are extremely heterogeneous. Successful preventive intervention focuses on more compact subgroups, specifically identified for prevention purposes — target groups or risk groups. Exchange. Organizers of preventive interventions must realize that the proposed behavior change is not viewed by the target audience as an unconditional good. Any significant change in behavioral patterns has its price (effort expended, attitudes of others, etc.), so the target audience's choice of whether or not to change behavior is determined by the perceived ratio of costs and benefits of the behavior change.

12. Models of Behavior Change Health Belief Model (HBM, 1950s), social psychologists of the U.S. Public Health Service: Perceived threat and awareness Perceived benefits of preventive behavior Perceived barriers to preventive behavior Perceived self-efficacy Stages of Change Model (SOC), Prochaska, DiClemente et al.; late 1970s; created based on an analysis of over 300 types of psychotherapies, describes the stages of forming motivation for healthy behavior: Stages of change (precontemplation, contemplation, preparation for action, maintenance of desired behavior, absence of temptation) Processes of change (awareness of the problem, awareness of negative emotions, critical self-assessment, social responsibility, determination) Decisional balance (analysis of potential benefits, analysis of potential costs) Self-efficacy (confidence in achieving results and overcoming obstacles, temptation to return to previous forms of behavior). Diffusion of Innovations Model, Rogers E., 1995, describes the patterns of spread of preventive intervention: Advantages of the innovation over alternatives. Compatibility of the innovation with human values and capabilities. Degree of simplicity and ease of perception and usability. Possibility of testing the innovation on a limited scale. Observability – the degree to which the results of the innovation are "visible" to other people, provoking its discussion with representatives of the target group, contributing to the diffusion of the innovation.

Today we conclude our first theoretical block. And as a summary, let's look at prevention in a broad social context as, well, essentially, I would say, an independent social institution, as a function of society aimed at preserving the health of society as a whole. And I want to start this conversation with this graph. This is a graph that shows the dynamics of the Earth's population. I don't claim that it is correctly scaled, but it generally conveys the essence. And the essence of this graph is that for almost all of human history, there were, well, relatively few people on Earth compared to today. And here we see that rapid growth begins, well, literally in the last 500-300, or 200 years. For clarity, I have provided some figures on the right. Today, 8 billion of us are recorded. And when modern teenagers, who are now, say, 16 plus or minus years old, were born, there were 7 billion of us. And at the turn of the century in 2000, there were just over six billion of us. When I was born in seventy-fifth year, there were 4 billion of us. That is, it's half as many as today. So, before my eyes, the Earth's population has doubled. Well, that is, everyone can compare the number of people in their birth year with how many of us live today and be surprised at how directly this growth is happening before our eyes. And it should also be borne in mind that, in addition to the number of people living, life expectancy has also rapidly increased over the past centuries. Today, Japan is the leader. There, I think, the average life expectancy is 83 years. In Russia, it is 73 years. But, for example, in some of the most disadvantaged African countries, it is about 35 years. But the fact is that about 100 years ago, the average life expectancy was 35 years even in Europe. That is, we are also observing a rapid increase in life expectancy, such an extension of all its stages, and accordingly, a change in the entire social structure, statuses, and social roles, and so on, and so forth. And, of course, such an unprecedented sharp increase in both the number of people living simultaneously and the increase in their life expectancy could not but affect all aspects of the life of every person and society as a whole. And therefore, today, in the 20th century, we observe many phenomena that have never occurred in human history. We are experiencing them for the first time. And these rapid social changes must be kept in mind when we talk about prevention. Perhaps we should start here by saying that, throughout human history, when a grandfather rocked his grandson in his arms, he could, in general, predict his fate quite accurately, because his grandson's fate was the same as his father's fate. His father's fate was the same as his father's fate, and so on, and so forth. That is, generation after generation, people remained in their social strata. And there were, in general, no great chances to change the life scenario that their ancestors lived. And today the situation is the opposite. We see the world completely differently compared to our teenagers. Well, for example, if only because the internet appeared before our eyes, mobile communication appeared, and, in general, we lived most of our conscious lives knowing nothing about them. And our children, they have already appeared in the digital world, as if it had always been that way. That is, from their point of view, life without the internet and life among dinosaurs are roughly equally long ago. The world is changing, its technologies, the nature of social relations so quickly that different generations feel completely different in it. And today, adults, that is, we, find ourselves in a difficult situation for the first time in human history, because it is not very clear what behavioral models should be passed on to the next generations, which ones will be adaptive tomorrow. Because the world is changing so rapidly before our eyes that the ideas about the world that always helped our ancestors and our parents, and even us, are already proving to be somewhat unsuitable today. And today, for the first time in human history, many elements of culture began to be passed not from older generations to younger ones, but vice versa, from younger to older. That is, for example, our children teach us how to use various services, gadgets, and so on. Well, simply because this is an integral part of the modern world, into which we have not had time to fit. Well, my child, for example, is trying to teach me programming, because he believes that without understanding the logic of programming, well, it's somehow strange to live in the modern world. And here it must be said that the world is changing so rapidly that even what teenagers are learning today is already becoming outdated before our eyes. And, for example, that undeniable conviction that the logic of programming needs to be understood and known, and which was a ticket to the IT world, to a world of, in general, relative well-being, today, with the advent of artificial intelligence, is also being somewhat questioned. That is, we are not keeping up with this race of skills that will be useful to us in the future. And that is why there is so much talk about what universal skills will always be important. And that is why you hear a lot of talk about so-called soft skills. This is precisely an attempt to identify those skills that will be useful in any case, no matter what technologies we have in our world. So. Well, or, for example, a high school student comes to an appointment and says that he has a conflict with his parents because he is a born musician, he really likes it. And his parents believe that this is not a profession, it is some kind of hobby, and they want him to be a lawyer. And from the parents' point of view, they are right, because all their experience and the experience of previous generations says that a lawyer is a person, a profession that will always feed you. And a musician is indeed something not serious. With the advent of artificial intelligence, for example, this situation may change, because today there are many startups where a computer tries to, well, be in the role of a lawyer, and it really has huge capabilities, because it immediately correlates each case with all the articles of legislation that exist, with all the huge number of precedents that have been in courts and which are also digitized and uploaded to special databases, and which quite quickly and accurately issues, accordingly, some legal opinions, impartial, objective, based on a larger and more accurate amount of information, on a more accurate understanding of legislation. And therefore, we can expect that many, well, professions in the field of law will also be greatly squeezed out by artificial intelligence. But musicians, on the other hand, that is, where, in fact, a living person is present and required - this is a creative profession. And creative professions will not be squeezed out by artificial intelligence. Well, because people come to a concert to listen to a living person. There is no point in going to a concert to listen to artificial intelligence. And therefore, it is very possible that in the very near future, the profession of a musician will turn out to be much more promising than the profession of a lawyer. And such changes in the sphere of culture and in the labor market have led to the need to reform the education system. What does it consist of and what is its logic? It must be said that the education system, as a social institution, was originally formed for the needs of industry. Industry needed a certain number of people who possessed a certain set of skills. And in essence, the education system was engaged in forming these skills, transmitting them from teachers to students. But as a result of the changes we discussed today, firstly, sharp changes occurred in the economic sphere. That is, if once the economy was mainly agrarian, in recent centuries, especially in the 20th century, the economy became mainly industrial, against which, in general, the education system was formed for the needs of industry, then in recent decades the economy has become generally intangible. All the main money revolves in the world of the intangible economy, and primarily in the service sector, in the sphere of managerial decision-making in information technologies, and in marketing, and so on, and so forth. And, accordingly, the market today requires some other qualities that allow a person to produce some product in this new intangible world. And therefore, in our practice, there have now appeared cases where adolescents conflict with their parents because they have different ideas about the need for education. That is, parents complain that children, figuratively speaking, do not read "War and Peace." And when you start to ask the children what they are actually doing during this time while they are not reading "War and Peace," it turns out that they are writing music for games, that they are running private servers for some companies, that they are running some blogs, and, most surprisingly, they are earning money, sometimes even more than their parents, while still being schoolchildren. Because throughout human history, well, at least relatively recently, for a person to earn well, they had to have means of production. And means of production were always in the hands of organizations, and large organizations at that. And a person had to study for a long time, and make a career there, only after which some social success came to them. And this is what is ingrained in the minds of us and older generations. And today, the means of production for teenagers have simply turned out to be, well, in their phones and their desktop computers. That is, the structure of the economy has turned upside down, and therefore the structure of learning values has also turned upside down. I don't mean to say that the value of "War and Peace" has become less today, but I want to say that the format of learning itself has changed very much. It has changed in three main ways. First, it was always believed that a person studies, acquires a profession for a long time, and this profession feeds them for the rest of their life. But today it turns out that it is impossible to acquire one profession in advance, because in a changing world, as we have already said, professions can suddenly lose their relevance, because new promising sectors of the economy are being created today at the intersection of different disciplines, different sciences, different spheres of the economy. For example, mathematical chemistry is a promising direction today. Who would have thought that before? And from this follows the second point that we must keep in mind - that a person in the modern world is forced to learn constantly, and constantly improve in their profession, and master many new related skills, because all of them will eventually combine into something more complex, something that will most likely be in demand by the market. And that is why in our practice there are often cases when parents come and complain that their child is studying somewhere, not finishing, grabbing one thing, grabbing another. And we, in our time, took things seriously, pursued them, brought them to a diploma, and all that. But teenagers act rationally from the point of view of today's world, because they come and learn different things, drawing, music, programming, whatever, but they come there to learn not to get a diploma, not to achieve some height in some specific field. They come there to take from it what they need to take, to the extent that they want to take it. And simply because they feel that it interests them. And to the extent that it interests them, they take something from that sphere. And, accordingly, with a high degree of probability, this skill will be very useful to them somewhere. They will add it somewhere to some main skill of theirs, some main profession of theirs, about which, by the way, they may not know anything at the moment. And therefore, today, in this changing world, in this changing market, it is best to focus not on those professions that were traditionally prestigious, profitable, and so on, but rather to focus on the child's own motivation, on what interests them, and to support this motivation. And the child themselves, based on their feelings, will assemble the set of skills, the set of knowledge and abilities that will be useful to them in the future. And this will probably be more optimal than if we guide them from the point of view of our already outdated experience. Here we come to the third, most important point, which I wanted to draw attention to and which is of great importance, in fact, for prevention. The third point of the education system reform is not based on the passive transfer of knowledge from teacher to student, but on the idea that knowledge is a complex product that is the effort of both teacher and student. They both participate in creating this complex product, which is knowledge in the modern world. And that is why today we talk so much about project-based learning and about various other ways of involving students in educational processes and in independent project work in general. And what does this remind us of? What we already, remember, talked about when we talked about health, that health today is also such a complex product that is the result of cooperation between doctor and patient. And why? Because the pattern of morbidity has changed. Because people today get sick and die primarily from chronic diseases. And this shift in the causes of mortality and morbidity mainly from an infectious to a chronic pattern occurred not only because people defeated, well, partly largely defeated infectious diseases, but also because, due to the demographic trends we discussed, there was such a personalization of responsibility for everything, for one's behavior, for one's actions. If throughout human history, control over people's behavior was mainly carried out by society, by various social institutions, then as public well-being grew, a person's life became less and less dependent on society. And, accordingly, a person began to rely more on their own choice, on their own preferences. But at the same time, a person began to bear greater responsibility for their behavior and for the results of their decisions. And thus, over the past centuries, well, in developed countries, at least, there has been such a transition, which sociologists, well, starting with Durkheim, called the transition from traditional society to, well, to a more modern one, to its different varieties. This transition consisted in the fact that human behavior became more autonomous, but also more responsible, and this also led to an increase in experienced stress. Because now, if something goes wrong, well, simply put, the person themselves is to blame, and not some cultural norms that they followed. And, accordingly, in the face of this experienced responsibility, a person experiences a greater level of stress, which also contributed to the development of chronic diseases. And, accordingly, this led to society's demand for psychology, for understanding one's behavior. Accordingly, that is why psychology received such a powerful impetus in its development precisely in the last 100 years. And, in all likelihood, the demand for psychology, for psychologists, will only grow in the near future. And it will continue to grow until people, en masse, learn how to manage their stress. And in essence, all our prevention is the organization of assistance to the population in overcoming their stress. Well, now, in light of all that has been said, what about adolescents? It is clear that raising younger generations has always been a difficult task, but today it has become even more complicated. Why? Because the demands in the modern world for what we call healthy and adaptive behavior have increased. And here we observe the same trend as we discussed regarding education and health. That is, that very healthy adaptive personality, that very healthy adaptive behavior that we want to achieve from adolescents, is also so complex today that it cannot simply be transmitted from older to younger generations, or imposed directly. It can only be a product, a result of joint efforts in which the adolescent themselves is directly involved and interested. And, accordingly, views on upbringing and prevention, on any preventive work among adolescents, are changing. In general, the result of any adolescent upbringing model is separation. That is, when an adolescent becomes independent, psychologically, socially, emotionally, materially. And in all senses, they represent such an already, well, independent personality. And how to achieve this when our world is becoming more and more complex and unpredictable? The only way out in such a situation is not to prepare the adolescent for some predetermined initial model of behavior, but to develop their own adaptive qualities, thanks to which they will already cope with the situations they encounter. And therefore, three trends have emerged in upbringing models, which are aimed precisely at developing independence. Firstly, it is care for the child's emotional sphere. This means that upbringing is carried out not through emotional pressure, but through some other more reasonable means. Secondly, it is the development of the cognitive sphere of adolescents and, the formation in them of an adequate rational picture of the world with all its pros, cons, limitations, and an understanding of their own responsibility for their actions and decisions. This is necessary so that the adolescent themselves finds a basis for making certain decisions not in some prescriptions, but in understanding what is generally happening around them, what is happening to them, and how to act correctly in certain situations, what would be good for them and for everyone around them. And the third direction is the formation of independent skills, the formation of independent behavior. That is, it means that the adolescent is given the freedom of independent behavior and the freedom of independent choice, as their awareness grows in all the situations they encounter. Well, because phrases like when parents tell an adolescent: "You'll be 18, then you can have your own opinion and decide things." This actually means that the adolescent is not allowed to act independently and is not allowed to prepare for what will happen to them when they turn 18. And at 18, by the way, boys are given automatic weapons. At 18, adolescents can already start their own families. And if they do not have sufficient experience of preliminary independent behavior, of making independent mistakes, of independent attempts to overcome these mistakes, then they will simply not be ready for the moment when they turn 18 and when legally they become, in general, fully responsible for their behavior. That is, all these three trends in the emotional, cognitive, and behavioral spheres are aimed at forming independent adaptive behavior, assuming that, well, no one will manage the adolescent better than they themselves. That is, the older an adolescent becomes, the less accessible they are to any control possibilities from adults. And essentially, we can rely more on them, on their awareness. But this awareness needs to be formed, and it needs to be done starting from a very young age. And, accordingly, developmental psychology and adolescent psychology and other related areas give us this necessary knowledge to help adolescents, in fact, form this awareness. So. But within the framework of this course, we will not dwell on these issues in detail; we will talk about it another time. Today it is simply important for us to outline this trend in upbringing strategies that exist today. We are now more interested in what all these trends mean for prevention itself in relation to adolescent deviance. Well, here's a simple question. What is the easiest way to change a child's behavior if they are doing something wrong? The answer: punishment. Punishment or some kind of restriction. Moreover, this is a biologically determined method; it is used by animals in the same way. And the first, most understandable and simple reaction of any adult is to create negative reinforcement so that it connects in the child with this negative form of behavior. From our point of view, so that the child no longer does this, so that even at the mere thought of repeating it, this feeling of anxiety would arise in their head, which arises as a result of punishment from an adult. Moreover, punishment can be not only physical, but also emotional.
